meta.title: Lunar Landing Site Navigator — Vizcachas fuera de órbita
meta.description: Will a lunar landing site have sunlight and a line of sight to Earth on a given date? An open, educational tool built with NASA/JPL Horizons data for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.
meta.learnTitle: Learn the science — Lunar Landing Site Navigator
meta.learnDescription: An educational module on lunar sky geometry: azimuth and elevation, horizons, polar illumination and communication with Earth, with classroom activities.

hero.title: Lunar Landing Site Navigator
hero.question: If I land at this place on the Moon on this date, will I have Sun, and will I be able to talk to Earth?
hero.lede: Near the lunar south pole the Sun and the Earth barely rise above the horizon, and any mountain can hide them. Our open tool takes a landing site and a date, finds where the Sun and the Earth are, draws them over the local horizon, and shows when there is power and when there is communication.
hero.figure: Sky view from the Intuitive Machines 2 site (Mons Mouton, 84.8° S) on 20 Nov 2026. The Sun stands only 6.5° above the horizon. The panel at the bottom shows the real horizon profile from LOLA terrain data.

problem.title: At the lunar south pole, sunlight and signal are scarce
problem.intro: Artemis and the commercial landers of NASA's CLPS program are heading to the lunar south pole, where ice is trapped in permanently shadowed craters. But the same geometry that preserves that ice makes the region hard to work in.

points.title: The Sun grazes the horizon
points.body: The Moon's spin axis is tilted only about 1.5° from the ecliptic. Near the poles the Sun never climbs more than a few degrees, so a crater rim or a hill can put a lander in shadow for days.

points.title: The Earth sits low too
points.body: Because the Moon always shows the same face to us, the Earth hangs almost fixed in the lunar sky. Seen from the pole it is close to the horizon, and libration slowly moves it up and down.

points.title: Power and communication decide the mission
points.body: Solar panels need the Sun above the horizon. Direct-to-Earth radio needs a clear line of sight. If a launch slips by a few days, both can change.

problem.hardIntro: The data already exists in NASA tools, but they are built for specialists. We tested them with one question: “does Shackleton crater get sunlight in November?”

hard.caption: Searching “moon” as the observer location lists Earth observatories with “Moon” in their name. Choosing the Moon requires knowing codes such as @301.
The answer to “is there Sun?” is an asterisk next to the date, explained about 70 lines further down, inside a 15-column table with mixed units.
When we searched for Shackleton, the south pole appeared as stretched stripes. Relief, light and shadow were impossible to read.

problem.conclusion: Horizons knows exactly where the Sun is, but none of these tools answers the question directly. We wanted one screen, one question, and numbers anyone can trust.

solution.title: One screen, one question, verified numbers
solution.intro: Pick a landing site and a date. The tool shows the Sun and the Earth over the local horizon, the Sun's elevation, the hours of sunlight and of Earth visibility in the coming days, and a countdown to the next sunset or Earthset.

pipeline.title: JPL Horizons
pipeline.body: Topocentric azimuth and elevation of the Sun and the Earth seen from each site, one sample per hour.

pipeline.title: LOLA terrain
pipeline.body: Elevation data from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter, turned into a 360° horizon profile per site.

pipeline.title: Precompute
pipeline.body: Scripts query Horizons, build the horizons and validate everything against JSON schemas and tests.

pipeline.title: Interactive app
pipeline.body: JavaScript, Vite and three.js read the precomputed JSON and compare each body against the horizon.

solution.pipelineNote: An optional live API (FastAPI) queries Horizons for any latitude and longitude on the Moon and answers in the same format.

features.title: 3D sky view
features.body: The Sun and the Earth at true angular scale over the horizon, with a 2D compass and elevation ruler as a fallback.

features.title: Solar elevation first
features.body: The Sun's height above the horizon is the most visible number on screen, because it drives solar power.

features.title: Timeline and countdown
features.body: A time player, a 7-day timeline of Sun and Earth visibility, and a live countdown to the next sunset or Earthset.

features.title: Scenario comparison
features.body: Two or three site–date scenarios side by side. The tool marks which has more Sun hours and which has more Earth hours, and leaves the decision to you.

features.title: Polar maps
features.body: Choose a historical mission, type coordinates, or click directly on a stereographic map of either pole.

features.title: Open and multilingual
features.body: MIT-licensed code, mobile layout, and an interface in English, Spanish, Hindi and Simplified Chinese.

shots: Details panel: azimuth, elevation, status and countdown for the Sun and the Earth, plus visible hours over the next 24 h, 7 days and 30 days.
Site selection: historical missions, specific coordinates, or a clickable polar map (USGS SIM 3316 mosaic).
Mobile layout of the sky view.
solution.validationTitle: How we know it is right
solution.validationBody: Every position comes from JPL Horizons, NASA's official ephemeris service, which already accounts for libration and the Moon's orbital variations. A validation panel and automated tests compare our values with saved Horizons answers and show the difference.
solution.limitsBody: The horizon silhouette uses real LOLA terrain only for sites with elevation data; elsewhere the app uses an ideal flat horizon and says so. The ground texture below the horizon and the stars are illustrative.
solution.learnTeaser: Want to understand the geometry behind each number?

data.software: three.js, Vite, Python, NumPy, Requests, rasterio, pyproj, Matplotlib, pytest, jsonschema, FastAPI, Uvicorn, HTTPX, Astro and Tailwind CSS. Sun and Earth images: Figma Community file “Space Elements”.
data.ai: We used Claude (Anthropic) as a coding assistant, with every change reviewed by a team member. The team logo was generated with ChatGPT. Translations other than Spanish were made with AI and have not been reviewed by native speakers. The numbers are not AI-generated: they come from JPL Horizons and are checked by automated tests.

learn.title: Reading the lunar sky
learn.lede: Six short ideas explain every number the tool shows. Each one comes with a figure, and the activities at the end turn them into classroom exercises. Suggested level: secondary school and early university.

concepts.title: 1. Azimuth and elevation
body: To say where something is in the sky, we use two angles measured from where we stand. Azimuth is the compass direction: 0° is north, 90° east, 180° south, 270° west. Elevation is the height above the horizon: 0° on the horizon, 90° straight overhead, negative below it.
These coordinates are topocentric: they depend on the observer's exact place on the surface. That is why the same Sun can be high at Apollo 11 and barely visible at the south pole at the same moment.
concepts.figure: Azimuth is measured along the horizon from north; elevation is measured upward from the horizon.

concepts.title: 2. The horizon is not flat
body: On an ideal, smooth Moon the horizon would sit at 0° in every direction. Real terrain raises it: a crater rim or a mountain can block several degrees of sky in a given direction.
The tool describes the horizon as 360 numbers, one per degree of azimuth, built from LOLA laser altimetry. A body is visible only if it is above the horizon in its own direction.
concepts.figure: The same Sun elevation can be visible over a plain and hidden behind a crater rim.

concepts.title: 3. No air, no refraction
body: On Earth, the atmosphere bends light and lets us see the Sun even when it is slightly below the geometric horizon. The Moon has no atmosphere, so there is no refraction, and the sky is black even at noon.

The Sun and the Earth are disks, not points. The tool counts a body as visible as soon as the upper edge of its disk clears the horizon: center elevation + angular radius > horizon elevation. The Sun's radius is about 0.25°, the Earth's about 1°.
concepts.figure: A body is visible when the top of its disk rises above the local horizon.

concepts.title: 4. Sunlight at the poles
body: The Moon's axis is tilted only about 1.5° relative to the ecliptic, so the Moon has almost no seasons. A lunar day, from one sunrise to the next, lasts about 29.5 Earth days.

At the equator the Sun rises high and stays up for about two weeks. At the poles it circles the horizon, never more than a degree or two above it. Some high ridges are lit most of the time, while deep crater floors never see the Sun: these permanently shadowed regions can hold water ice.
concepts.figure: Near the equator the Sun climbs high; at the pole it skims along the horizon all day long.

concepts.title: 5. The Earth hardly moves in the lunar sky
body: The Moon is tidally locked: it turns once on its axis for every orbit, so it always shows the same face to Earth. Seen from the near side, the Earth stays in roughly the same spot of the sky, going through phases instead of rising and setting.

Libration, a small wobble in how we see the Moon, moves the Earth around that spot by up to about 7° to 8°. Near the edge of the near side and at the poles, that is enough to make the Earth rise and set over weeks.
concepts.figure: Libration makes the Earth trace a small loop in the lunar sky over about a month.

concepts.title: 6. Talking to Earth
body: Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication needs a straight line between the lander's antenna and the Earth, with no terrain in between. When the Earth is below the horizon, the lander needs a relay satellite.
On the far side the Earth is never visible. That is why China's Chang'e 4 and Chang'e 6 missions used the Queqiao relay satellites. The tool shows this as Earth hours equal to zero.
concepts.figure: With the Earth above the horizon the signal travels directly; otherwise it needs a relay in orbit.

glossary.def: Horizontal direction, measured clockwise from north (0°) to 360°.
Angle above the local horizon; negative means below it.
Measured from a point on the surface, not from the center of the body.
A table of positions of celestial bodies over time. JPL Horizons generates them.
The apparent wobble of the Moon that lets us see about 59% of its surface from Earth over time.
Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter, an instrument on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter that mapped the Moon's elevation.
Permanently shadowed region: crater floors near the poles that never receive direct sunlight.
Direct-to-Earth: communication between the lander and Earth with no relay.
Commercial Lunar Payload Services, the NASA program that buys deliveries to the Moon from companies.
About 29.5 Earth days, from one sunrise to the next at the same place.

learn.activitiesIntro: Each activity takes 20 to 40 minutes and needs only a browser. Open the tool in another tab.

activities.title: A lunar day at Apollo 11
steps: Choose Apollo 11 in the tool and pick today's date.
Move the date slider one day at a time and write down the Sun's elevation each day.
Plot elevation against date. How long until the Sun sets? How long is a full lunar day?

activities.title: Equator or pole?
steps: Compare Apollo 11 (near the equator) with Intuitive Machines 2 (Mons Mouton, near the south pole) on the same date.
Note the maximum Sun elevation and the Sun hours over 7 days for each site.
Use the tilt of the Moon's axis to explain the difference.

activities.title: Can we call home?
steps: Open Chang'e 4, which landed on the far side of the Moon.
Look at the Earth hours over the next 30 days. What do you see?
Research the Queqiao relay satellite and explain why the mission needed it.

activities.title: The launch slipped
steps: Pick a south-pole site and a date. Create a second scenario at the same site two weeks later.
Compare Sun hours and Earth hours in the scenario comparison.
Write a short recommendation for a mission that needs power more than communication, and another for the opposite case.
